The last piece, it's the advice I always give people when they're early in their career is to go find a company that's going to do super well. That one experience is going to transform your entire career. Having the logo on your resume, the people you meet, the experience you get financially. But that begs the question, how do you find that? How do you pick a company? I think in your advising today, you join later where it's a little more obvious. "Okay, they're doing great." Do you have any advice or lessons about how to identify earlier where to go work and how to be lucky in that pick?
turns.zh: 那里头有太多我想展开细聊的点了。最后那一点，也是我总给早期职业的人提的建议：去找一家会做得特别好的公司。那一次经历，会彻底改写你的整个职业生涯。简历上的那个 logo、你遇到的人、你在财务上得到的历练。但这就有个问题了：你怎么找到那样的？你是怎么挑公司的？我觉得你现在的顾问工作里，你进得比较晚，这时候往往明显些，"哦，他们做得很好"。你有没有什么建议或心得，关于怎么在更早的阶段识别出该去哪儿、怎么在那次选择里"撞上好运"？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Isn't that the billion-dollar question? So I worked for-
turns.zh: 这难道不是那个价值十亿美元的问题吗？所以我曾在——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For investing too.
turns.zh: 投资也是一样。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Yeah. I worked at Atlassian, which was phenomenal. Then I worked for Classy, which was a company that helped nonprofits raise money.
turns.zh: 对。我在 Atlassian 工作过，那家公司太棒了。后来我去了一家叫 Classy 的公司，是帮非营利组织募款的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've used that product.
turns.zh: 我用过那个产品。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Thank you. And we were acquired by GoFundMe. And it was fine, but it was no Atlassian. And then I spent the next five years trying to figure out, how do you pick your next Atlassian? So my advice would be for people earlier in their careers, it's easy to pick the winners if you go work for a big company that's a winner. I would love to work for Tesla, or AWS. Or right this second, I would die kill for a job at OpenAI. You know some of the big companies that are successful... Salesforce has totally been a career maker to so many top executives. (00:12:04): So early in your career, working for big name high momentum companies. I think you can't wimp out. You've got to want it and go for it. And maybe you apply year after year, and you meet people, and you try for it early in your company. (00:12:19): Later in your career, I think what you just said, picking later stage versus earlier stage gives you a better view of their momentum. I actually have a Post-it note, got it here, about what I look for. 10 parts of what would evaluate to see-
turns.zh: 谢谢。我们后来被 GoFundMe 收购了。那家公司还行，但跟 Atlassian 没法比。之后我花了五年时间琢磨：你怎么挑出下一个 Atlassian？所以我的建议是，对职业生涯早期的人来说，如果你去一家已经是大赢家的大公司，挑赢家就很简单。我特别想去特斯拉，或者 AWS 工作。或者就在此刻，我拼了命也想进 OpenAI 工作。你认识一些成功的大公司……Salesforce 对很多顶尖高管来说，完全就是个" career maker"（成就职业生涯的地方）。（00:12:04）所以在职业早期，去为那些大名鼎鼎、势头正猛的公司工作。我觉得你不能怂，你得真心想要、去争取。也许你年年都去投，去认识人，趁早去你公司里争取。（00:12:19）到了职业中后期，就像你刚才说的，挑偏后期阶段的公司比早期阶段的，能让你更看清它们的势头。我其实有张便利贴，就在这儿，写着我看重的点。评估一家值不值得去，有十个维度——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You just have that Post-it note around?
turns.zh: 你就随时把这便利贴带在身边？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I do. It's one of five Post-it notes on my board.
turns.zh: 对，带。我白板上有五张便利贴，这是其中一张。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to hear what the rest are too. But keep going.
turns.zh: 我也想听听另外几张是什么。你接着说。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I have to look at it for advisory. I only take eight to 10 clients. I'm always full. And so it has to be a phenomenal company. So how do I know if it's a phenomenal company? Here's my list. Rule of 40, which is your profitability and your costs together. The quality of the investors. Are they really top tier investors? Are they mid tier or some you've never heard of? Investors do a lot of due diligence, but you also want to look at their most recent rounds, because they could have phenomenal early stage and have slowed down. I think the later the size, the more reliable, because they've just made it farther. (00:13:23): Their Net Promoter Score or their customer satisfaction. Do people really rapidly love this product or is it like meh? Their net dollar retention, which is, how fast is their revenue growing? And I should have it on my Post-it note, but Snowflake was the benchmark. I think they were growing at 142%.
turns.zh: 我做顾问要用它来对照。我只接八到十个客户，永远都是满的。所以必须是非常了不起的公司才行。那我怎么判断它是不是了不起的公司？这是我的清单。40 法则（Rule of 40），也就是你的盈利能力和成本加在一起看。投资人的质量。他们是顶级投资人吗？中等，还是你听都没听过？投资人会做很多尽职调查，但你也要看他们最近几轮的融资，因为他们早期可能很厉害，后来却慢下来了。我觉得轮次越后期，越可靠，因为他们已经走得更远了。（00:13:23）还有他们的净推荐值（NPS）或客户满意度。大家是真的迅速爱上这个产品，还是觉得"呃，还行"？他们的净收入留存率（net dollar retention），也就是营收增长有多快？这应该写在我便利贴上，但我偷懒没写——Snowflake 是基准线。我记得他们当时增长 142%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think at one point it was 180, whatever.
turns.zh: 我记得有段时间是 180，随便吧。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Yeah. That sounds right. 180, 165. Net dollar retention, if you have a customer and they just renew at the same dollar rate, it would be 100. So 180 is almost doubling just their customers. So they didn't even need new customers, almost doubled their business. A phenomenal net dollar retention means it's a really strong healthy business. (00:14:09): I looked at their growth rate last year, their burn rate, are they going to run out of money? And then ideally, are they number one in their market? Do they have a Forrester or a Gartner Magic Quadrant? People tell you if they're number one. (00:14:22): And then the last thing is I look at their Glassdoor. Is it just a bad place to work and where people unhappy? Because they don't actually survive as long as companies where people are happier.
turns.zh: 对，应该是这个数。180、165。净收入留存率的意思是，如果你有一个客户，他只是按同样的金额续费，那就是 100。所以 180 意味着光靠老客户就几乎翻倍了。也就是说他们几乎不需要新客户，业务就快翻倍了。超高的净收入留存率，意味着这是一门非常健康、强劲的生意。（00:14:09）我还会看他们去年的增长率、烧钱速度，他们会不会把钱烧光？然后理想情况下，他们是不是市场第一？他们有没有 Forrester 或 Gartner 魔力象限？别人会告诉你他们是不是第一。（00:14:22）最后一点，我会看他们的 Glassdoor。是不是个糟糕的工作场所、大家不开心？因为那些地方，其实不如那些员工更开心的公司活得久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this list. You should turn it into a blog post, and there's another idea for you. Can you share what the other Post-its are around you? Even broadly.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这份清单了。你应该把它写成一篇博客，这也是给你多一个选题。你能说说你周围那几张便利贴都是什么吗？哪怕大致说说。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I can. One says, "More Yoda, less Wonder Woman," which basically is ask better questions. The second one was-
turns.zh: 可以。一张写着"多当尤达，少当神奇女侠"，说白了就是问更好的问题。第二张是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ask them backwards too.
turns.zh: 把它倒过来读也行。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Yeah, right? Ask them backwards. Which is funny, because the other Yoda thing I have up Is... Here wait. "Do or do not. There is no try." Backwards. I have another one that says, "Hell yes or no." When opportunities come to you and you're like, "Should I do this or should I not do this?" You only have so much time in your life. And so if it's not something that really excites you and gives you energy, it's tough to be the best at it. And so hell yes or no. (00:15:26): And then the last one is, "Worrying is wasted energy," because I think we live in this economic pressure cooker, and there's a lot of fear and uncertainty. But we just need to take that fear and uncertainty and thank it for giving us urgency. And then make the list of what can we control now and what should we do next.
turns.zh: 对吧？倒过来读。有意思，因为我贴的另一张尤达的话是……等下。"做，或不做，没有试一试。"反过来说。我还有一张写着"Hell yes，否则就别"（要么超兴奋，要么就拒绝）。当机会降临，你纠结"我该做还是不该做"的时候——你这辈子时间就那么多。所以如果一件事不能真的让你兴奋、给你能量，你很难把它做到最好。所以，要么超兴奋，要么就别做。（00:15:26）最后一张是"担忧是浪费能量"，因为我觉得我们活在这个经济压力锅里，有太多恐惧和不确定。但我们只需要把那恐惧和不确定接住，谢谢它们给了我们紧迫感。然后列一张清单：现在我们能控制什么，接下来该做什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's actually a perfect segue to my next question. And by the way, that was amazing. I'm glad that I asked about your Post-its. That's a whole life philosophy right there in Post-its.
turns.zh: 这其实正好能过渡到我的下一个问题。顺便说，刚才那段太精彩了。很高兴我问了你的便利贴。那几张便利贴，就是一整套人生哲学。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Yeah, I should do a BeReal. This is what is looks like at this side. These are all the Post-its.
turns.zh: 对，我该发个 BeReal（社交软件）。这就是我这边的样子。全是便利贴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So the question is around, I don't know if we're technically in a recession, but maybe we're on the verge of recession. The market's not great. And a lot of people are being laid off, or have been laid off, or are worried about being laid off, or just graduating college and looking for jobs. And I'm curious if you have advice for people trying to find a job in this market or just generally trying to accelerate their career. What is your advice for just how to deal with this environment while also trying to advance your career?
turns.zh: 好。那我的问题是，我不知道我们现在技术上算不算衰退，但也许正处于衰退边缘。市场不太好。很多人在被裁、已经被裁、或者担心被裁，或者刚大学毕业在找工作。我很好奇，对于想在这种市场里找工作、或者只是想加速自己职业生涯的人，你有什么建议。面对这种环境，你既想推进职业生涯，又该怎么应对？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I'd like to take in two parts. One is if you're unemployed and one is you're in a job. So if you're unemployed, it's tough. It's a tough time. There's a lot of supply. And so I think you just really need endurance and grit. And the sticker worrying is wasted energy, because you will get another job. It's just going to be a little bit more of a bumpy ride than some other years. (00:16:55): And the best executives I know have had down periods in their careers, where they were out of work for a while, where they were fired by a CEO, who this or that. And what they have in common is endurance. They're just back in the ring. So I think it's important to not lose endurance. (00:17:15): It's also important not to settle on a crappy job or a crappy company. Each job you have prepares you for the next job, and each logo you have prepares you for the next job. (00:17:27): So I'd spent a lot of my career trying to also chase waves. My first job in college, I was in nonprofit, and then I wrote a book on the giving programs of the top 50 tech companies. And I realized that tech companies had a bunch of money in 1999, and were giving it away to charities. And I wanted to go into tech, because that's where the growth and money was. And I thought I could give it back to the world and good, but I could be inside the bubble. (00:17:55): And then within tech, I moved my way to B2B. And within B2B, I moved my way to SaaS. And within SaaS, I've moved my way into dev tools, and collaboration, and now AI. (00:18:05): There's this book called The Millionaire Next Door, which talks about how the very best antique store makes one or 2% profit. And the very worst oil and gas company makes 35% profit. And we know that some of the worst software companies make 65% profit. (00:18:25): So picking your industry will propel your career, and picking the right company will propel your career, and then doing a good job will propel your career. So I think that there's no magic bullet to getting a job. But working your network, sticking with it, and continuing to grow your skills are the three most important things.
turns.zh: 我想分两部分说。一部分是如果你失业了，一部分是如果你有工作。如果你失业了，这很难，是个艰难的时期，供给很多。所以我觉得你真的需要韧性和 grit（咬牙坚持）。回到那张"担忧是浪费能量"的便利贴，因为你一定会再找到工作的，只是路会比某些年份颠簸一点。（00:16:55）我认识的最好的高管，职业生涯里都有过低谷期——有阵子没工作、被某个 CEO 炒了之类。他们的共同点就是韧性，他们就是会重新回到擂台。所以我觉得重要的是别丢掉韧性。（00:17:15）同样重要的是，别将就一份烂工作或者烂公司。你做的每一份工作，都是在为下一份工作做准备；你简历上的每一个 logo，都是在为下一份工作铺路。（00:17:27）所以我职业生涯里很大一部分，是在追"浪"。我大学第一份工作是在非营利组织，后来我写了一本书，讲全美前 50 家科技公司的公益项目。我意识到 1999 年科技公司很有钱，在把钱捐给慈善机构。我想进科技行业，因为那是增长和钱所在的地方。我觉得我可以既回报世界，又待在泡沫里面。（00:17:55）然后在科技行业里，我一路挪到了 B2B。在 B2B 里，挪到了 SaaS。在 SaaS 里，挪到了开发者工具、协同，现在是 AI。（00:18:05）有本书叫《邻家的百万富翁》，讲到最好的古董店只赚百分之一二的利，而最差的油气公司能赚 35% 的利。而我们知道，最差的软件公司能赚 65% 的利。（00:18:25）所以选对行业会推动你的职业生涯，选对公司会推动你的职业生涯，然后好好干也会推动你的职业生涯。所以我觉得找工作没有魔法子弹。但经营人脉、坚持到底、持续提升技能，是最重要的三件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Big part of this conclusion is don't feel like your career needs to slow down in this period.
turns.zh: 你这段结论里很重要的一点是：别觉得你的职业生涯在这个阶段就得慢下来。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: And I think if you're in a job, some of my greatest career growth came in the economic downturns. In the 2000s, in the 2008. Because other people take their foot off the gas, and you can put your foot down. If you're willing to learn more, hit yourself into new roles or new responsibilities that no one's covering at your company. When they don't hire tons of people for everything, there's lots of open projects where you can raise your hand and grow. You just can't be as focused on title and salary right now. You're kind of building up value that you'll be able to monetize on the other end of this recession or downturn.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果你有工作，我一些最大的职业成长恰恰来自经济下行期。2000 年那会儿，2008 年那会儿。因为别人都松了油门，而你可以踩下去。如果你愿意学更多、把自己塞进公司里没人覆盖的新角色或新职责。当公司不大量招人做所有事的时候，有很多敞开的项目，你可以举手去接、去成长。只是你现在不能太盯着头衔和薪资。你是在积累价值，等这轮衰退或下行过去之后，你就能把它变现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's segue to chatting about growth. And I thought it'd be fun to start with your story of running some very expensive ad campaigns. I know the founders are always kind of flirting with this idea of buying a bunch of billboards, running TV ads, maybe subway ads and bus ads. And you've done a lot of that and you've spent a lot of money doing that, and particularly non-digital advertising. And so I'm curious what you've learned from your experience and approach to this sort of marketing spend.
turns.zh: 咱们转到聊增长吧。我觉得从一个有趣的地方切入：你跑过一些非常贵的广告战役的故事。我知道创始人们总在琢磨要不要买一堆广告牌、投电视广告，或者地铁、公交广告。你干过很多这种事，也砸了很多钱，尤其是非数字广告。所以我很好奇，从你的经验和做法里，关于这种营销投入，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Yes. I've spent hundreds of millions of dollars on it actually. I ran global awareness advertising for Oracle, and did all of the airports, and the front page of the Wall Street Journal, on the back page of The Economist, and take over in the middle of Salesforce in downtown San Francisco. And we did the Ironman movie sponsorships, and the sports teams and arena sponsorships.
turns.zh: 对，我其实在这上面花了几亿美元。我在 Oracle 负责过全球品牌认知广告，做了所有机场广告、华尔街日报头版、经济学人封底，还有在旧金山 downtown 的 Salesforce 大楼整栋包下。我们还赞助了《钢铁侠》电影，赞助了运动队和场馆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds very expensive.
turns.zh: 那听起来超级贵。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Super expensive. And then Atlassian to a lesser degree, we spent several million dollars on different awareness campaigns to get chat noticed, or to associate Jira with the Atlassian brand. Advertising is sexy and super expensive for the benefits. It's a multi-year benefit of awareness. People have to see things many times, and it has to really resonate with them. (00:20:45): So my advice to founders is that the most important thing is the quality of your product. Oracle spent a ton of money, and people still didn't like us in a lot of ways because they had poor experiences with the salespeople, or they didn't like Larry, or the product had kind of languished since it had been acquired by the company. So your product has to really be fantastic. And then also to do good brand advertising, it has to be sustained over a long period of time. (00:21:14): So Oracle had the front page of the Wall Street Journal, back page of The Economist, this boring advertising template with the red bar, but it made it memorable. We would do market tests, and two or three or 10 times more people would recognize the Oracle brand without the logo, because of the consistency versus SAP or or IBM. (00:21:35): So you really need to be thoughtful about spending consistently over a longer period of time, and a smaller amount on a fewer number of things can be really effective. So Snowflake, for instance, has always gotten credit for doing a billboard on 101, and people think they do lots of advertising. But for many years, it was only the billboard on 101. It was just sustained and strategic.
turns.zh: 超级贵。然后 Atlassian 也做过，规模小一点，我们花了几百万美元做不同的品牌认知战役，要么是让 HipChat 被注意到，要么是让 Jira 跟 Atlassian 这个品牌挂钩。广告很诱人，也很贵，但带来的好处是长线的——它是好几年的认知积累。人们得看好多遍，而且它得真的打动他们。（00:20:45）所以我对创始人的建议是：最重要的还是你产品的质量。Oracle 砸了好多钱，但很多方面人们还是不喜欢我们，因为他们跟销售打交道的体验很差，或者不喜欢拉里（Larry），或者产品被公司收购之后就停滞了。所以你的产品必须真的出色。然后要做好的品牌广告，它必须长期持续下去。（00:21:14）Oracle 有华尔街日报头版、经济学人封底，那个带红条的无聊广告模板，但恰恰让它被人记住。我们做市场测试，因为一致性，认出 Oracle 品牌的人（即使没 logo）比 SAP 或 IBM 多出两三倍、甚至十倍。（00:21:35）所以你真的要深思熟虑：在长期里持续、稳定地花钱，而且少而精——在更少的事情上花更少的钱，反而可能非常有效。比如 Snowflake，大家一直夸它在 101 公路上立了块广告牌，人们以为他们投了很多广告。但其实好多年里，就只有 101 公路上那一块牌子。只是它持续且讲策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I guess two things that I take away from that is one, you can spend a lot of money, and if your product's not actually incredible, it's not really going to do much. And correct me if I'm wrong. And then two is sometimes, just one very targeted spend is worth a lot more than just blanketing a bunch of ads.
turns.zh: 我从你那总结两点：第一，你可以砸很多钱，但如果你的产品不是真的牛，其实也起不了太大作用。不对的话请纠正我。第二，有时候，就一笔非常精准的投入，比铺天盖地一堆广告值钱得多。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Absolutely. I was telling you a story that at Atlassian, we did a big advertising campaign on our HipChat product, which was head-to-head with Slack, and it was an Office Space spoof with Bill Lumbergh. But the product had some uptime issues, and some feature issues, and Slack pulled ahead, and the advertising wasn't what would've made it or broken the product. It's really the product experience, and the advertising just amplifies.
turns.zh: 完全对。我刚跟你讲了个故事：在 Atlassian，我们给 HipChat 这个产品做了个大广告战役，它当时是跟 Slack 正面对打，是个《上班一条虫》的恶搞，用了 Bill Lumbergh 那个角色。但产品当时有些宕机问题、一些功能问题，Slack 就跑到前面去了，而广告并不是那个能成就或毁掉产品的东西。真正起决定作用的是产品体验，广告只是放大器而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you also shared with me this HipChat ad, that's maybe my favorite billboard ever. And I don't even know why looking back, but it made me laugh so hard. Back in the day, it was this meme of some early meme stick figure guy saying, "Why you no use HipChat?" Looking back I'm like, "Okay. I don't know how funny." But I think in the moment that was a really popular meme, and it really stuck with me.
turns.zh: 我觉得你还给我看过那个 HipChat 的广告，可能是我有史以来最喜欢的一块广告牌。回头看我都不明白为什么，但它真的让我笑到不行。那时候是个早期的梗图：一个火柴人小人说着"你为什么不试试 HipChat？"。现在回头看，我心想"好吧，不知道当时有啥好笑的"。但我觉得在那个当下，那是个超火的梗，而且它真的印在我脑子里了。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Well if you think about the best advertising, it's something that has a little twist of humor, or personality, or truth that sticks in your brain. So yes, that was a successful advertising. And kudos to my team, because of course I don't write it myself as the head of marketing. But yeah. (00:23:22): And some of my other favorite ads are also others that highlight the customer. So New Relic did an advertising campaign around data nerds. When data nerds were not really popular, they were still nerds. And they had these tattoos that said nerd life, and they featured customers on billboards talking about cool data nerds. And some of those campaigns that really stand out have something that's funny, unexpected, and then true to the product.
turns.zh: 如果你想最有用的广告是什么，就是带一点幽默、或者个性、或者真实感的那种，能黏在你脑子里。所以是的，那是个成功的广告。给我团队点个赞，因为作为营销负责人，我当然不是自己写的。不过没错。（00:23:22）我另一些最爱的广告，是那些凸显客户本身的。比如 New Relic 做过一个围绕"数据书呆子"的广告战役。那时候数据书呆子还不流行，他们还是书呆子。他们有纹身写着"nerd life"（书呆子人生），还把客户放上广告牌，讲那些很酷的数据书呆子的故事。那些真正出彩的战役，都有点好笑、出人意料，而且对产品来说是真的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember those, one of the ads featured, our CTO at Airbnb, Mike Curtis, and everyone was very excited to see his face on the Billboards.
turns.zh: 我记得那些。其中一张广告用的是我们在 Airbnb 的 CTO，Mike Curtis，大家看到他出现在广告牌上都特别兴奋。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Yeah, Salesforce has done a great job with those over the years too, really highlighting the customers.
turns.zh: 对，Salesforce 这些年也把这点做得很好，真的在凸显客户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So zooming out a little bit, you specialize working with companies that are going through hypergrowth. And you've worked with companies like Miro, Segment, Bill.com, which I don't know if people know is just a massive, massive business. And also 1Password. (00:24:21): And on the topic of 1Password, interestingly I didn't realize how big and how fast 1Password has been growing. And just last week I saw this report from Okta where they have all this interesting data about which products people are using, and they put out this report showing which products you're getting the most new customers. And then on a different axis, which companies are getting the most users per new customer. (00:24:46): And there's this six companies in this quadrant. Figma, Miro, Snowflake, Sentry, HubSpot, and 1Password, which blew my mind. And interestingly, you work with two of them. And so all that to say, what have you noticed about what is most in common with companies that are going through hypergrowth? What is most in common in terms of what has contributed to them being that successful?
turns.zh: 稍微放大一点看，你专长于跟正在经历超高速增长的公司合作。你合作过的公司包括 Miro、Segment、Bill.com——我不确定大家知不知道 Bill.com 是个超级、超级大的生意。还有 1Password。（00:24:21）说到 1Password，有意思的是，我之前没意识到它增长得又大又快。就上周，我看到 Okta 的一份报告，里面有很多关于大家在用什么产品的有趣数据，他们出了份报告，显示哪些产品拿到了最多新客户；然后换一个维度，哪些公司每个新客户带来的用户数最多。（00:24:46）有个象限里有六家公司：Figma、Miro、Snowflake、Sentry、HubSpot，还有 1Password，这让我惊掉下巴。而有趣的是，你正好跟其中两家合作。所以说了这么多，你注意到那些正在超高速增长的公司的共同点是什么？在促成它们成功这件事上，最大的共同点是什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: The biggest thing is an amazing product that people love to use. I mean ChatGPT is the most hypergrowth product that we've seen in history potentially, because people are so excited to use it and it's working in interesting ways. So Miro, whiteboards were the number one most uploaded asset in Jira forever. Because people all get together and they write their ideas on a whiteboard, and then they need to remember it and iterate on it. And that bringing that concept to life just hit a cord that people wanted to use. And when one person uses it, another person uses it. (00:25:42): 1Password similarly, I've been a 1Password user for more than 10 years. We used it at Atlassian, as a corporate. And then they have the family plan. So I used it at home and then my dad got elderly, so I had a family that I was the administrator for, and then I go into different companies and you bring it with you. (00:26:02): And one of the other companies I advise is Productboard. And I became an advisor of Productboard because 1Password's CPO had it in another company, brought it into 1Password, rolled it out company-wide to get alignment and visibility on the product roadmap. (00:26:18): So in order to get hypergrowth, you have to have organic, inbound, and viral word of mouth. You can't pay enough to grow at those rates and have a viable company, especially in this economic efficiency market. So has to be an amazing product, has to have some viral activity. So we just talked about Miro or Atlassian. You could have an individual person use it and then they say, "Hey, I'm going to present at this meeting with Miro, come join me on my board. I've got these confluence pages we'd set up as a wiki about these engineering topics, and I want your team to collaborate on them." So those natural points where your users are selling to other people is way more efficient than having sales people that have to sell to other people. (00:27:12): And then I think the third thing is really riding the lightning, I would call it. So hypergrowth companies go through the stages of growth that would take other companies five years or 10 years. They're going from 10 to 50, they're going from 50 to 100, they're going from 100 to 200, they're jumping. And so they really need to keep hiring 2X and 3X leaders who have seen the next stage of growth. And then the people inside can be homegrown talent, but it's tricky to keep up. (00:27:46): So my whole business is based on people who are trying to be homegrown leaders, but don't know what the next stage of growth looked like. And so a lot of hypergrowth companies hire ahead, hire advisors. Leaders need to really think about mentors and friendships of people who know what great looks like at the next scale, because it's going to be here before you know it. And so I would say those things. Amazing product, viral movement, and company that can ride the lightning.
turns.zh: 最关键的，还是一款大家都爱用的好产品。我的意思是，ChatGPT 可能是我们有史以来见过增长最猛的产品，因为大家用得特别起劲，而且它的使用方式确实很有意思。比如 Miro，白板在 Jira 里长期是上传量第一的素材。因为大家聚在一起，把想法写在白板上，然后需要记住它、在上面迭代。把这个概念变成现实，正好击中了人们想用的那个点。一个人用了，另一个人也用。（00:25:42）1Password 也一样，我用它超过十年了。我们在 Atlassian 作为公司也在用。然后他们有个家庭套餐。所以我在家用，后来我爸老了，我成了管理那个家庭套餐的管理员，然后我进不同公司，又把它带过去。（00:26:02）我顾问的另一家公司是 Productboard。我成为 Productboard 的顾问，是因为 1Password 的 CPO 在另一家公司用过它，把它带进了 1Password，然后全公司铺开，让产品路线图获得对齐和可见性。（00:26:18）所以要实现超高速增长，你必须具备有机增长、自然流入和病毒式口碑。你靠砸钱是没法维持那种增速，同时还做一个能活下去的公司的，尤其在这个讲究经济效率的市场里。所以必须有个好产品，必须有点病毒式传播的动能。刚聊了 Miro 和 Atlassian。可以是一个普通人用了，然后他说"嘿，我要用 Miro 在这个会上演示，来我的白板一起吧。我搭了这些 Confluence 页面当工程主题的维基，我想让你们团队一起在上面协作。"所以那些你的用户在替你向别人推销的自然节点，比靠销售去推给别人的效率高太多了。（00:27:12）然后我觉得第三点是，我称之为"迎着闪电奔跑"。超高速增长的公司，把别的公司要花五年、十年的成长阶段压缩在很短时间里走完。它们从 10 到 50，从 50 到 100，从 100 到 200，一路跳着涨。所以它们真的需要不断招那种能带领 2 倍、3 倍规模团队的领导者，因为他们见过下一个成长阶段。而公司内部的人可以是自己培养的人才，但要跟上很难。（00:27:46）所以我的整个生意，就是建立在那些想当"自己培养的领导"、却不知道下一个成长阶段长什么样的人身上。所以很多超高速增长的公司会提前招人、招顾问。领导者真的要去想：找那些知道下一个规模上"最好长什么样"的人当导师、当朋友，因为那个阶段很快就会到来。所以我会说这几点：惊人的产品、病毒式的扩散、以及一家能迎着闪电奔跑的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine founders listening to this that don't have insane virality or huge word of mouth are like, "Is there no path to being a really successful company?" And then I think about companies that did succeed with other channels, like say paid or SEO. And so I guess the question for you is, do you need to grow in this environment, I guess, primarily through word of mouth, organic reality, growth engines? Or do you still see opportunity for companies to grow other ways, say paid, or SEO, or sales eventually?
turns.zh: 我想象一下，正在听这期、自己没有疯狂病毒传播或巨大口碑的创始人，大概会想："难道就没有成为一家真正成功的公司的路了吗？"然后我会想到那些靠别的渠道成功的公司，比如付费或者 SEO。所以我想问你的是：在这种环境里，增长是不是主要得靠口碑、有机的、自然的增长引擎？还是说你依然看到公司有其他方式增长的机会，比如付费、SEO，或者最终靠销售？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: For sure. All of the things are important. I think what I wanted to say first as you were talking was that it's easy to look at a company after they've been viral and be like, "That's amazing." I would like to start a newsletter. I have. It's carilu.com. Lenny has a newsletter. How can I ever grow like Lenny's virality? But Lenny started with one blog, and then another, and the consistency. (00:29:14): And when I look back at Atlassian, people would be like, "It must have been so easy to go from 100 to 500 million." And it never felt easy. It was a slog to do exactly what you're talking about. New features, listen to customers, strong SEO. Actually SEO was the number one marketing motion that we used, and SEM. We spent probably between 15 and 25% of our leads from paid search marketing at the time. Now I have a ton of customers that are pretty deep into account-based marketing. (00:29:49): Getting to virality and getting the hypergrowth is not a magic bullet. It's consistency, customer obsession, incremental improvements across all parts of the business. So I think founders just need to double down on having a product that's differentiated and does something that their customers really love. And each incremental step is a step forward.
turns.zh: 当然。所有这些都重要。我想先说的一点是，你刚说的——很容易在一家公司已经病毒传播之后去看它，然后说"太厉害了"。我也想开个newsletter。我已经开了，在 carilu.com。Lenny 也有 newsletter。我怎么可能长得像 Lenny 那么病毒？但 Lenny 是从一篇博客开始的，然后第二篇，靠的是一致性。（00:29:14）回头看 Atlassian，人们会说"从 1 亿到 5 亿肯定特别容易吧"。但当时从来没觉得容易。做的正是你说的那些苦活：新功能、听客户、强 SEO。其实 SEO 是我们用的第一营销动作，还有 SEM。当时我们大概 15% 到 25% 的线索来自付费搜索营销。现在我很多客户都深入做基于客户的营销（ABM）了。（00:29:49）达到病毒传播、达到超高速增长，不是魔法子弹。是持续性、对客户痴迷、业务每个环节的增量改进。所以我觉得创始人只需要死磕一件事：做一个有差异化、客户真的爱的产品。每往前走一小步，就是前进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Coda. You've heard me talk about how Coda is the doc that brings it all together and how can help your team run smoother and be more efficient. I know this firsthand because Coda does that for me. I use Coda every day to wrangle my newsletter content calendar, my interview notes for podcast, and to coordinate my sponsors. (00:30:35): More recently, I actually wrote a whole post on how Coda's product team operates, and within that post they shared a dozen templates that they use internally to run their product team. Including managing the roadmap, their OKR process, getting internal feedback, and essentially their whole product development process is done within Coda. (00:30:53): If your team's work is spread out across different documents and spreadsheets and a stack of workflow tools, that's why you need Coda. Coda puts data in one centralized location regardless of format, eliminating roadblocks that can slow your team down. Coda allows your team to operate on the same information and collaborate in one place. Take advantage of the special limited time offer just for startups. Plan up today at Coda.io/lenny and get a $1,000 startup credit on your first statement. That's Coda.io/lenny to sign up and get a startup credit of $1,000. Coda.io/lenny. (00:31:32): Say that you as a company are seeing word of mouth in some virality, and you want to think about accelerating that, leaning into word of mouth. Obviously you want everyone to be talking about how awesome you are sharing with their friends. Is there anything that you've seen as a good way to lean into word of mouth and accelerate it?
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Coda 赞助。你听我说过 Coda 是如何把一切整合在一起的文档，怎么帮你的团队运转更顺、更高效。这是我 firsthand（亲身）知道的，因为 Coda 就是这么帮我的。我每天用 Coda 来打理我的 newsletter 内容日历、播客采访笔记，以及协调赞助商。（00:30:35）最近，我其实写了一整篇帖子讲 Coda 的产品团队怎么运作，里面他们分享了十几个内部用来运转产品团队的模板。包括管理路线图、他们的 OKR 流程、获取内部反馈，基本上他们整套产品开发流程都在 Coda 里完成。（00:30:53）如果你团队的工作分散在不同文档、表格和一摞工作流工具里，那就是你需要 Coda 的原因。Coda 把数据放在一个集中位置，不管什么格式，消除了拖慢团队的障碍。Coda 让你的团队在同一份信息上操作、在一个地方协作。趁现在面向初创公司的限时特别优惠：今天就去 Coda.io/lenny 注册，首单账单可享 1000 美元初创额度。就是 Coda.io/lenny 注册拿这 1000 美元初创额度。Coda.io/lenny。（00:31:32）假设你作为一家公司，已经看到一些口碑和病毒传播，你想加速它、靠向口碑。你显然希望每个人都聊你多牛、分享给朋友。你有没有看到过什么好办法，能靠向口碑并把口碑加速？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I think there's two or three things. One is really empowering the people in your company to be thought leaders. So early days, Atlassian's founders were on all the developer boards. And in fact, I remember, we were maybe 150 million or 200 million, and Scott Farquhar the CEO was still participating and going back and forth in different dev forums when I was like, "I don't know, should we elevate your status? Should we have evangelists and engineers that do this?" (00:32:18): And we did, right? And look, one of my clients now is Weights & Biases, the ML ops company helping lots of different AI companies with their ML models. And they have really thoughtful technical people who know more and write more on the blog and engage with their community. And that creates a word of mouth, because they're providing both a product and concepts and learning. That's one of the HubSpot secrets was all of their really thoughtful, helpful content, certifications for marketers. (00:32:52): So I think going back to summarize, word of mouth can be driven by thought leadership, which is hiring the right people to really be deeply engaged as super experts. Having a really strong content strategy that's either in communities that already exist, online communities, open source communities. (00:33:13): And then third I would say building your own community. So no one sells your product better than your own happy customers. And if I go way back to the very beginning of my career, I worked on a marketing team where I owned demand gen just for net new prospects, and a peer owned demand gen just for existing customer upsell. And we would have different field events. (00:33:34): And the existing customer ones were smaller than if we'd invited the prospects and had more buzz. And the prospect ones were very salesy. Whereas if we brought them together and you had customers talking to each other and prospects listening, everyone had a better time. (00:33:48): So Atlassian, one of our secrets was this amazing user group community where we just paid for beer and a pizza, and we'd facilitate local in-city leaders, and people would meet up and talk about our products, and talk about development generally, and grow their careers and grow their network. So I think those are the three. The right people, the right content, and the right communities.
turns.zh: 我觉得有两三件事。一是真的赋能你公司里的人成为思想领袖。早期，Atlassian 的创始人混在所有开发者论坛里。事实上我记得，我们大概 1.5 亿或 2 亿的时候，CEO Scott Farquhar 还在不同开发论坛里来回参与，当时我就想"我不知道，我们要不要抬升一下你的身份？要不要让布道师和工程师去做这个？"（00:32:18）我们确实这么做了，对吧？你看，我现在一个客户是 Weights & Biases，那家做 ML ops 的公司，帮很多不同的 AI 公司搞定他们的 ML 模型。他们有真正有想法的技术人，懂更多、在博客上写得更多、跟社区互动。这就创造了口碑，因为他们既提供产品，也提供概念和知识。HubSpot 的秘诀之一，就是他们那些真正有想法、有帮助的内容，还有给营销人的认证。（00:32:52）所以总结一下：口碑可以由思想领导力驱动，也就是招对的人，让他们作为超级专家深度参与。再就是有个很强的内容战略，要么进已有的社区——线上社区、开源社区。（00:33:13）第三，我会说是建立你自己的社区。没人比你自己的满意客户更能卖你的产品。回到我职业生涯最开始，我在一个营销团队，我负责只针对全新潜在客户的需求生成，一个同事负责只针对老客户增购的需求生成。我们会办不同的线下活动。（00:33:34）老客户的活动，如果只邀请老客户、少了那种热闹，规模会小一些。而潜在客户的活动，特别销售味。但如果我们把两拨人放一起，让客户互相聊、潜在客户在旁边听，大家反而都更尽兴。（00:33:48）所以 Atlassian 的一个秘诀，就是我们那个超棒的用户组社区——我们就出钱买啤酒和披萨，扶持城市本地的负责人，人们聚在一起聊我们的产品、泛泛聊开发，发展自己的职业和人际网。所以我觉得就是这三点：对的人、对的内容、对的社区。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As you were talking, I was reminded, I was just chatting with the founder of Gusto about their journey early on. And he said that for the first 200 customers, he sat there with them running payroll, watching how they react every step of the payroll process and how they feel at every moment. And that was a big part of what helped them build the product that people actually continue using, and love, and stick with. And if it wasn't in person, it was on a phone call. And it's like the epitome of doing things don't scale, just like for hundreds of new customers watching them use your product. Pretty wild.
turns.zh: 你说话的时候，我想起来，我刚跟 Gusto 的创始人聊了他们早期的历程。他说前 200 个客户，他都是坐在他们旁边帮他们跑工资单，看他们在工资单流程每一步怎么反应、每个瞬间是什么感受。那正是帮他们做出人们真的持续用、爱上、留下来不走的产品的一大原因。如果不是面对面，也是在电话上。这就像"做那些无法规模化的事"的极致——就那样看着几百个新客户用你的产品。挺疯狂的。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I mean that's the secret. That's the secret sauce. And I've heard some early stage startup advisors say that you should build processes that don't scale first. Because when you're in the super early stage seed A under 10 million, you've really got to go deep at that stage. (00:35:04): And in fact, I see that that's one of the problems that companies experience as they get much bigger, when product managers can't meet with customers, or they get limited customers, or maybe they can only meet with a junior user, only the administrator, and not lots of the users. So that insight into the daily struggles and experience of your customers, it's harder to get as you get bigger I think.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，那就是秘密。那就是秘方。我听一些早期初创顾问说过，你应该先建那些无法规模化的流程。因为你在超早期、种子轮、A 轮、一千万以下的时候，那个阶段你真的得往深里扎。（00:35:04）事实上，我看到这是公司变大之后会遇到的问题之一：产品经理见不到客户了，或者只能见有限的客户，或者只能见一个初级用户、只见管理员，见不到大量用户。所以那种对你客户日常挣扎和体验的洞察，公司越大反而越难获得，我觉得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to drill into Atlassian. You've brought them up a couple times. You were at Atlassian for a long time. You were there from early days of growth to IPO. And one of the most interesting elements of Atlassian and something that comes up a lot on this podcast is product led growth. (00:35:44): And Atlassian I think is one of the most classic examples of a product led growth company. And from what I understand, y'all waited a long time to hire your first salesperson. So my question is what did you learn from that experience about when is the right time to start leaning into sales and hiring sales, and what are the trade-offs of waiting longer or doing it earlier?
turns.zh: 我想深挖一下 Atlassian。你提了好几次。你在 Atlassian 待了很久，从早期增长一直到 IPO。Atlassian 最有趣、也在这档播客里经常被提到的一点，是产品驱动增长（PLG）。（00:35:44）我觉得 Atlassian 是产品驱动增长公司最经典的例子之一。据我所知，你们等了非常久才招第一个销售。所以我的问题是：从那个经历里，关于"什么时候才是开始靠向销售、招销售的正确时机"，你学到了什么？以及等得更久和更早做的取舍分别是什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Atlassian was a super unique company at a super unique point in time, because the founders never took outside money except for one late stage financing to buy out some early employees, to give some liquidity. So we never had VCs or private equity that had a voting share that was significant, that could overrule the founders. (00:36:28): So the founders were going through this experiment that turned out to be really successful, where they took all the money they would've spent on a sales org and plowed it into engineering and product. I'm going to pull up a slide here that tells the Atlassian story about the ratio of the sales and marketing to the product and engineering.
turns.zh: Atlassian 是一家在独特时间点的独特公司，因为创始人从来没拿过外部钱，除了一次后期融资用来回购一些早期员工的股份、给他们一点流动性。所以我们从来没有什么有实质表决权的 VC 或私募股权能推翻创始人。（00:36:28）所以创始人当时在做这个后来被证明极其成功的实验：把本来会花在销售组织上的所有钱，全部砸进工程和产品中。我调出一张幻灯片，讲 Atlassian 的故事——关于销售营销和产品工程的投入比例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And by the way, check this out on YouTube if you're listening to this and check out this slide.
turns.zh: 太棒了。顺便说，如果你在听这期，去 YouTube 看看这张幻灯片。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: So this is a representative sample of what we did in Atlassian's history, and what ratios still exist today, even several years later. Where we spend way less on sales and marketing. Marketing spent less than other marketers. And also we had almost no sales org, or a sales org that was really focused on renewals, or now an assisting sales org that's focused more on enterprise. But relative to other companies, a much smaller, much more efficient sales org. And we took all that money and put it into product. So here we're spending two times, three times as many dollars in R&D as many other companies that we'd benchmark against to make a product that really sold itself.
turns.zh: 这是 Atlassian 历史上我们做过的事、以及即使几年后今天依然存在比例的一个代表性样本。我们在销售和营销上花得少得多。营销比其他营销人花得少。而且我们几乎没有销售组织，或者那个销售组织真的只聚焦于续费，或者现在是个辅助性销售组织，更聚焦大企业。但相对于其他公司，我们的销售组织小得多、高效得多。我们把那所有的钱都投进了产品。所以这里我们在研发上花的钱是很多对标公司的两三倍，就为了做出一个真的能自我销售的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. So I'm looking at the slide. And again if you're listening, check this on YouTube because it's pretty crazy. This slide of bar chart of spend in sales and marketing and R&D, and Atlassian is the very lowest amount of spend in sales and marketing, and the highest spend in product. And it's interesting that it's from 2020, so it's not even in the early days. It's like still today basically.
turns.zh: 有意思。我看这张幻灯片。再说一次，如果你在听，去 YouTube 看，因为这挺疯狂的。这张销售营销和研发支出的柱状图，Atlassian 在销售营销上的支出是最低的，在产品上的支出是最高的。而且有趣的是这是 2020 年的，所以甚至不是早期了，基本就是今天的状态。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Right. I'm going to close this down and keep telling you a little bit more about it. There's some unique things that people can take now and incorporate. So the real strategy in sales, sales is the most expensive vehicle, right? Expensive people that spend a lot of time. So the Atlassian model was to sell only to people who were already customers really. If several people or a couple groups had purchased, we'd help them with their renewals. And now in the later incarnations of our sales orgs at Atlassian, it helps a lot more with larger enterprise companies who need enterprise deals, or does more cross-sell and upsell, but doesn't really do prospecting. Net new prospecting is a really expensive way to get new customers. (00:38:51): So we see different trends coming now with companies, because almost no one can do pure product led growth. Because your investors want to see accelerated growth, and most people believe that adding an SDR or adding an AE will add a predictable amount of revenue. And so it's difficult because product led growth and sales have to coexist. (00:39:16): But the whole transition in marketing that's happening to account-based marketing and intent-based signals is trying to do some of what we were doing at Atlassian, only to engage salespeople with customers that are actually likely to buy. And if you look at other hyper-growth companies, Airtable, Miro, both of those I know from the inside have had strategies where the salespeople really only engage after some threshold has been hit of number of users that have already been paying for the product on their credit card. But sometimes it's a high number of 20, 40 people at an account have to be engaged before a salesperson engages.
turns.zh: 对。我把这个关掉，再跟你多讲一点。有些独特的东西，大家现在就能拿去用。销售这件事，销售是最贵的载体，对吧？昂贵的人，花大量时间。所以 Atlassian 的模式是：只卖给那些已经是客户的人。如果好几个人或几个团队已经买了，我们帮他们续费。而在 Atlassian 销售组织后来的形态里，它更多地帮那些需要企业级交易的大公司，或者做更多交叉销售和增购，但不真的做陌生开发。纯新客户的陌生开发，是获取新客户非常贵的一种方式。（00:38:51）所以我们现在看到公司里出现不同趋势，因为几乎没人能做纯产品驱动增长了。因为你的投资人想看到加速增长，而大多数人相信加一个 SDR（销售开发代表）或加一个 AE（客户执行）就能增加一笔可预测的营收。所以这很难，因为产品驱动增长和销售必须共存。（00:39:16）但营销正在向基于客户的营销（ABM）和基于意图的信号转变，本质上就是在试图做我们在 Atlassian 做的事——只在那些真的可能会买的人身上，才让销售介入。你看其他超高速增长公司，Airtable、Miro，这两家我从内部知道，它们的策略是：销售真的只在某个阈值被突破后才介入——也就是已经有若干个用户用自己的信用卡给产品付过费。但有时候阈值很高，一个客户账户里得有 20、40 个人参与，销售才会介入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Based on that, what is it you recommend to founders these days that maybe are product led and just self-service [inaudible 00:40:00] oriented. Do you kind of take this experience and wait as long as you can to hire your first salesperson? I know it's very specific to the situation, but what kind of advice do you generally give?
turns.zh: 基于这点，你 nowadays 给那些可能是产品驱动、只做自助[听不清 00:40:00]的创始人什么建议？你会把这段经验拿过来、能等多久就等多久再招第一个销售吗？我知道这很看具体情况，但你一般会给什么建议？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: You and I are both like [inaudible 00:40:14] who was just on your podcast earlier this month. Product led growth depends so much on your product and your buying market. There's some buying markets that are less likely to use salespeople, and you need to go in from the beginning. HR might be one, right? Whereas a lot of the hyper-growth companies in the dev tool space can use product led growth because developers both hate failed people, and really love to research themselves. So you see [inaudible 00:40:47] taking off because people engage and kind of self sell. (00:40:52): So I would recommend, get closer to their customers and read the signals. If your product is good enough, the people can get time to value in a couple of days instead of weeks or months. You can have a product led growth motion. If your product needs to be put in context, and customized, and assisted, sales teams sometimes are expensive services arms to cover over product issues and help customers buy it until it's fixed. Or if you're in a market where your buyer just really doesn't buy online with research and a demo, then you need to have salespeople. But I would say try not to hire too fast and too far ahead in sales and inside sales, because it seems like it's going to add revenue, but it actually is a huge cost and a huge drain on the business if the product isn't getting that kind of resonance.
turns.zh: 你跟我都像[听不清 00:40:14]——他这个月初刚上过你播客。产品驱动增长太取决于你的产品和你的购买市场了。有些购买市场不太会用销售，你得从一开始就走那条路。HR 可能算一个，对吧？而很多开发者工具领域的超增长公司能用产品驱动增长，因为开发者既讨厌被销售缠，又特别爱自己研究。所以你看到[听不清 00:40:47]起飞，因为人们自己参与、自己把自己卖出去。（00:40:52）所以我建议：贴近客户、读信号。如果你的产品足够好，人们能在几天而不是几周或几个月内获得价值，你就能做产品驱动增长。如果你的产品需要放进具体场景、需要定制、需要辅助，销售团队有时是昂贵的服务臂，用来盖住产品问题、帮客户买，直到产品修好。或者如果你所在的市场里，你的买家就是不在线研究加个 demo 就买，那你就得有销售。但我会说，别在销售和内部销售上招得太快、太超前，因为它看着像能增加营收，但如果产品没达到那种共鸣，它对业务其实是巨大的成本和巨大的拖累。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I just had a conversation with the founder of Retool for this series that I'm working on, and he basically found the same thing you found where they thought it could be a product led experience where you're building internal tools using their product, but it turned out nobody really understood how to do it themselves and it took a lot of handholding to make it work. So they became sales led from the beginning, even though it feels like a tool that has a lot of potential to be product led and self-service.
turns.zh: 我刚跟 Retool 的创始人聊了我在做的那个系列，他基本发现了跟你一样的事：他们原以为能是产品驱动体验——你用他们产品搭内部工具，但结果发现没人真明白怎么自己弄，得大量手把手才跑得起来。所以他们从一开始就是销售驱动，尽管它感觉像个很有潜力做产品驱动、自助的工具。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I think the other hybrid I'm starting to see is people who turn their SDR, sales development reps, into sales engineers, researchers. So instead of having a salesperson who's like, "Would you like to have a meeting with another salesperson?" The first touch for customers that are maybe kicking the tires or trying a product led growth is a person who can help guide them on the path. And I like this hybrid nature because basically it extends product led growth, but helps people in this case where you're talking, where the product itself isn't so intuitive that you can get all the way to the buy itself.
turns.zh: 我觉得我开始看到的另一种混合，是把 SDR（销售开发代表）变成销售工程师、研究员。所以不是那种"你想跟另一个销售见个面吗？"的销售，而是客户第一次接触时——那些可能在试试水、或在试产品驱动增长的人——是个能帮他们在路上指引的人。我喜欢这种混合，因为它本质是延展了产品驱动增长，但在你说的那种情况里帮到人：产品本身没直观到能一路自我卖到成交。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It also sounds more fun to talk to a sales engineer than a salesperson.
turns.zh: 听起来跟销售工程师聊也比跟销售聊有意思。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I know. I always wanted to be a sales engineer. I was a salesperson, and I crushed on the sales. Engineering team who knew everything and could draw all the architectures.
turns.zh: 我知道。我以前一直想当销售工程师。我当过销售，但我 crush on（迷恋）那个什么都懂、能画出所有架构的销售工程团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow, I didn't know that. A couple more questions around this stuff. So you've worked with a lot of different companies. And you kind of come in and help them figure out ways to grow faster, unlock growth opportunities. What do you find often gets most in the way of making big changes to the way they approach growth and approach different growth channels? And maybe on the flip side, what do you find is most essential to making big changes at a company around how they think about growth?
turns.zh: 哇，我不知道这个。围绕这些我再问几个问题。你跟很多不同公司合作过。你进去帮他们找出更快增长、打开增长机会的办法。你最常发现，是什么最阻碍他们对增长方式、对不同增长渠道做大刀阔斧的改变？反过来，让一家公司在"怎么想增长"上做大改变，最必不可少的是什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: The big growth levers are pretty consistent across companies. You start with one product, and you have a couple choices on how the go-to-market works. Product leg growth or sales assisted. You get a little bit bigger and you add an incremental product, or you start to add new segments. You're going to focus on a vertical like finance, or you're going to go global, or you're going to add new sales channels like a partner channel. (00:43:56): And what I've seen with the big growth levers is that it can't ever be an individual department's goal without being a cross company strategy goal, if it's really going to make a difference. (00:44:07): So you've talked about it in your newsletter and on your podcast, but growth isn't just like a person in the engineering team that hacks by themselves. It really has to be funded and thoughtfully constructed so that there's the right content and experience, and product features, and virality features a customer to continue to drive growth. (00:44:29): And similarly, lots of companies right now are trying to move upmarket because the economy has created so much pressure in S&B that they're going to try to move to enterprise, or they've trying not to sell as much just to tech companies because tech companies are under pressure and so they want to move to different parts. (00:44:51): Sometimes the marketers get blamed or sales gets blamed, we don't have enough leads. But really it's a company strategy problem where the company hasn't decided, "Hey, we're going to all move in this direction and if we're going to sell the enterprise, marketing's going to bring in leads, products going to have a roadmap, and some meaningful features to enterprise. The customer research is going to start thinking about them. We're going to hire some customer support people who know how enterprises work. We're going to hire some salespeople who sell differently to enterprises than S&B." The big growth levers are strategy problems, not individual departmental problems.
turns.zh: 大的增长杠杆在公司之间相当一致。你从一款产品起步，对怎么走向市场有几种选择：产品驱动增长，还是销售辅助。你再大一点，就加一款增量产品，或者开始加新细分。你会聚焦某个垂直领域，比如金融；或者走向全球；或者加新销售渠道，比如伙伴渠道。（00:43:56）而我看到的关于大增长杠杆的是：如果它真要起作用，它绝不能是某个单独部门的目标，而必须是跨公司的战略目标。（00:44:07）你在你的 newsletter 和播客里也聊过，但增长不只是一个工程团队里自己黑进去的人。它真的需要被出资、被精心构建，这样才有对的内容、对的体验、对的产品功能、对客户的病毒功能，持续驱动增长。（00:44:29）类似地，现在很多公司想往上走（upmarket），因为经济给 SMB（中小企业）造成太大压力，他们想试走向企业级；或者他们不想只卖给科技公司，因为科技公司承压，所以他们想挪到不同板块。（00:44:51）有时候市场部被怪、销售被怪：我们线索不够。但其实这是个公司战略问题——公司没决定"嘿，我们要一起朝这个方向走，如果我们要卖企业级，市场部要带线索进来，产品部要有路线图、有对企业级有意义的功能。客户研究要开始想他们。我们要招些懂企业怎么运作的客户支持。我们要招些跟 SMB 不同方式卖企业级的销售。"大的增长杠杆是战略问题，不是单独部门的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what do you find needs to happen for that to change? Is that like CEO needs to be like, "Here's what we're doing, everyone get on board," or something else?
turns.zh: 那你觉得要改变这个，需要发生什么？是 CEO 得说"这是我们要做的，大家跟上"，还是别的什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I think it can come either way in the C-suite, right? So my job, I advise hypergrowth CEOs and CMOs of companies, 30 million to 500 million. Often if I'm advising a 30 to 100 million company, the more junior marketer with a CEO who's often a first time founder, who doesn't necessarily know if the marketer's good or not. Hasn't done run marketing before, doesn't know if they should trust what the marketers saying. (00:46:04): So often the marketer is saying," Hey, we're having problems because the company's not delivering on this promise you want us to sell." And sometimes the CEO doesn't know if they can trust it, a judgment. And so in that case, someone like me who's an advisor comes in and is like, "That's right, it's not a marketing problem, it's company strategy problem. Let's have an offsite and build some OKRs where we all go after enterprise and we win it together." (00:46:30): You'll see at bigger companies or when a new CMO comes in with more senior or seasoned, they'll have the social capital to push back into the executive suite. Or a new head of engineering who will say, "Look, I know you want to move ahead faster, but we actually have to catch up on this technical debt." And they'll push back and get that strategic space that they need. So it can either come from the CEO or it can come from the C-suite really coming together to solve those problems, instead of pushing them under the rug.
turns.zh: 我觉得从 C 级高管层哪边来都行，对吧？我的工作，是给 3000 万到 5 亿的超高速增长公司的 CEO 和 CMO 做顾问。通常如果我顾问的是 3000 万到 1 亿的公司，那个比较初级的市场人配的 CEO 往往是第一次当创始人，他不一定知道这市场人好不好。他以前没管过营销，不知道该不该信市场人说的。（00:46:04）所以常常市场人会说："嘿，我们遇到问题，因为公司没兑现你想让我们卖的那个承诺。"而有时候 CEO 不知道该不该信，这是个判断。所以那种情况下，像我这样的顾问进去说："对，这不是营销问题，是公司战略问题。我们搞个 offsite（外出务虚会），建一些 OKR，大家一起冲企业级、一起赢。"（00:46:30）你会在更大的公司、或者一个新 CMO 带着更资深老练进来时看到，他们有社会资本去推回高管层。或者一个新工程负责人会说："看，我知道你想更快往前，但我们其实得先把技术债补上。"他们会推回、拿到他们需要的战略空间。所以它既可以从 CEO 来，也可以从 C 级高管真正聚到一起解决那些问题——而不是把它们压到地毯下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on this nuance that a lot of times, there's not a lot of trust between the marketing head and the CEO. And I'm curious what you find helps build that trust.
turns.zh: 你刚点到一个微妙处：很多时候，营销负责人和 CEO 之间没什么信任。我好奇你觉得什么能帮建立那种信任。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: There's a couple things that are really critical for senior marketers, and I actually have a blog coming up based on a podcast I've recorded about why CMOs mostly get fired. And the issues are generally one, that the CMO isn't focused enough on the revenue. So some CMOs get focused more on the pipeline or the awareness, and the CEO doesn't feel like they really have a partner in driving the revenue. Or they don't feel like the CMO really has a handle on what will drive the revenue. (00:47:46): So marketing's tough because it's a big spend category, and lots of the spend doesn't convert in quarter. Some of it doesn't convert in year. Advertising campaigns, some take multiple quarters. (00:47:57): So it's really important for CMOs to have a handle on the metrics, a solid prediction of what growth levers they can use, and to be able to talk in the terms of the CEO and the board. (00:48:11): And I think that that's the biggest gap that I generally see. And then of course, there's a whole bunch of table stake stuff. They have to be running their business well. They have to be a good leader that people want to work for. They have to hire a great team that elevates them and the company, they have to be thoughtful and strategic about the market space that the company's in. They're not just working the levers in the factory. They're thinking, "What new markets should we enter? What new growth areas should we employ?" Like we just talked about. "What new companies should we acquire?" They also need to be thinking ahead. And I think being good on metrics, good on strategy, and good on market helps CMOs spar with CEOs in a way that builds trust.
turns.zh: 对资深营销人来说，有几件事真的非常关键。我其实有篇即将发的博客，基于我录的一期播客，讲的是"为什么大多数 CMO 被炒"。问题一般就那几个：一是 CMO 对营收不够聚焦。有些 CMO 更聚焦在管道（pipeline）或品牌认知上，CEO 不觉得他们真有个能一起驱动营收的搭档；或者不觉得 CMO 真的懂什么能驱动营收。（00:47:46）所以营销很难，因为它是个大支出类，而且很多支出当季度不转化。有些一年都不转化。广告战役，有些要好几个季度。（00:47:57）所以对 CMO 来说，牢牢掌握指标、对自己能用什么增长杠杆有个扎实预测、并且能用 CEO 和董事会的语言说话，真的很重要。（00:48:11）我觉得这是我一般看到最大的缺口。当然，还有一大堆基本盘：他们得把业务管好；得是个大家愿意为之工作的好领导；得招一支能抬升他们和公司的一流团队；得对公司所在的市场空间有想法、有战略，不只是工厂里扳杠杆的人。他们要想"我们该进什么新市场？该用哪些新增长领域？"就像刚聊的。"该收购哪些新公司？"他们还得往前看。我觉得在指标上出色、在战略上出色、在市场上的出色，能帮 CMO 跟 CEO 过招，从而建立信任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that you say, that blog post you titled Why Most CMOs Get Fired, and it connects with something. Casey Winters noted, that most CPOs also get fired chief product officers. I forget the quote, but it's something like, "The most you can help for is a couple swings at the bat before you get fired as a CPO." Why do you think this is so common for these chief C-suite roles to startups to not work out?
turns.zh: 有意思你说了，你那篇博客标题叫《为什么大多数 CMO 被炒》，它跟一件事连上了。Casey Winters 提到过，大多数 CPO（首席产品官）也被炒。我忘了原话，但大概是"作为 CPO，你在被炒之前最多就几次挥棒的机会"。为什么你觉得这种事在初创公司的这些 C 级角色上这么常见、这么不灵？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: They're incredibly hard jobs. The chief product officer and the chief marketing officer are both strategy jobs with difficult to measure results because some of them are direct and some of them are indirect. And I think both of them get swept up when a company's not performing well too. If company's not performing well, you can kind of swap out the head of product, and the next one will be more strategic and deliver faster. (00:49:55): And in fact, I've worked in one of the roles, the CFO was really after my chief product officer, and ultimately got him fired because he wanted to move everything offshore, and develop faster, and he didn't want to re-platform, and he didn't want to deal with the technical debt. And the CFO was sure that it was the CPO's fault, and then they got rid of the CPO, and the CFO tried his plan and it didn't work. And then you bring someone in who's like, "No, that guy had the right plane." (00:50:21): So both of them are tough jobs. And they require a high bar of excellence, a high connection of trust, and then I think just endurance to keep going and find the next role where you're really a fit and the company really has momentum.
turns.zh: 这些都是极难的工作。首席产品官和首席营销官都是战略岗，结果难衡量，因为有些直接、有些间接。而且我觉得，当公司表现不好时，这两个人也都会被卷进去。如果公司表现不好，你大概会把产品负责人换掉，下一个会更战略、交付更快。（00:49:55）事实上，我待过其中一个角色，当时 CFO 真的盯着我那个首席产品官，最后把他搞下台了——因为 CFO 想把所有东西挪到离岸、更快开发，而 CPO 不想重建平台、不想处理技术债。CFO 确定是 CPO 的错，然后他们把 CPO 踢了，CFO 试了自己的计划，没成。然后你再招个人进来，说"不，那哥们儿方向是对的"。（00:50:21）所以这两个都是苦活。它们要求极高的卓越标准、高度的信任连接，然后我觉得还需要韧性，继续走、找到下一个你真合适的、公司真有势头的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It also reminds me, I was just talking to, I think it was Canva. Where their first engineering hire is now their CTO still, and their first marketing hire is their CMO still. So it does work out on occasion.
turns.zh: 这也让我想起，我刚跟——我认为是 Canva——聊过。他们第一个工程 hire 现在还是 CTO，第一个营销 hire 现在还是 CMO。所以偶尔也是能成的。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: It works out on occasion. And in fact, I've been playing around with a 10 part series about those CMOs in the CMO world, because there's about 10 to 15 CMOs who have started when it's really small and grown all the way. And they're the ones we really want to learn from. And I know a lot of them and really admire their work, and have learned so much.
turns.zh: 偶尔能成。事实上我一直在捣鼓一个关于那些 CMO 的十部分系列，因为在 CMO 圈里，大概有 10 到 15 个 CMO 是从真的很小就开始、一路长到很大的。那些才是我们真该跟学的。我认识很多，真的很佩服他们的工作，也学到太多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You should absolutely do that. That sounds very cool. You talked about how you work with companies from 30 million to 500 million. What is it about that stage that's unique, and what happens after 500 million, and what's the difference before say 30 million? I know it's not an exact number, but how do you think about that range?
turns.zh: 你绝对该做那个。听起来很酷。你聊过你跟 3000 万到 5 亿的公司合作。那个阶段有什么独特之处？5 亿之后又发生什么？3000 万之前又有什么不同？我知道不是精确数字，但你是怎么看这个区间的？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: No, it's not an exact number. My bottom number is because there's this early stage of product market fit where the founder and the company are trying to figure out who their real ideal customer profile is, and can they sell to them consistently? (00:51:39): So I've worked for some early stage startups where we've tried lots of different things, but they're not repeatable. You can't scale it. "This product works for this. This product works for this too and it works for this," but those are all kind of unique cases studies. And so my skill is in helping people scale. (00:52:00): And so if they've already found product market fit and they've gotten some funding or they're bootstrapped, but have enough funding to really be trying to build out marketing in a marketing team, that's when I know what each stage looks like. So I know what $30 million great teams look like, and 50 million, and 100, and 150 million, 200 million. My ride at Atlassian was from about 100 to 500. (00:52:26): And then over 500, the act of going public, being an early stage public company, I know what that all looks like. And then beyond that, there's public company consultants I think more, that do more specific things. I more help the CMO and CEO structure for the next stage of growth, because they're going through it so fast, they haven't hired someone yet who's already seen.
turns.zh: 不，这不是精确数字。我那个下限，是因为有这么个早期的产品市场契合（PMF）阶段，创始人和公司还在摸索：谁才是他们真正理想的客户画像？能不能稳定地卖给他们？（00:51:39）所以我待过一些早期初创，我们试了很多不同的东西，但都不可复制。你没法规模化。"这个产品对这个管用。这个产品对这个也管用、对那个也管用"，但那些都是独特的个案。而我的本事是帮人规模化。（00:52:00）所以如果他们已经找到 PMF、已经拿到融资或者自给自足，但有足够的钱真的去搭一个营销团队，那就是我知道每个阶段长什么样的时候。我知道 3000 万、5000 万、1 亿、1.5 亿、2 亿的优秀团队长什么样。我在 Atlassian 是从大概 1 亿到 5 亿。（00:52:26）然后超过 5 亿，上市、做早期上市公司，那些我知道长什么样。再往上，我觉得更多是上市公司的顾问在做更具体的事。我更多是帮 CMO 和 CEO 为下一个增长阶段搭结构，因为他们冲得太快，还没招到那个已经见过下一阶段的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. One very nuanced question I want to ask you is about bundling. So there's HipChat and Slack kind of ate their lunch, not necessarily through bundling, but there's Slack. And then Slack, I don't know if it's true, but it feels like Microsoft Teams is eating their lunch with bundling. And I'm curious, what do you think of bundling as a strategy to win long-term? And also, how do you compete against say, a Microsoft that may one day bundle your product for free, and you might be in big trouble?
turns.zh: 明白了。我想问你一个很微妙的问题，关于捆绑（bundling）。HipChat 是被 Slack 抢了饭碗，不一定是靠捆绑，但就是有 Slack。然后 Slack，我不知道是不是真的，但感觉上 Microsoft Teams 正靠捆绑抢 Slack 的饭碗。我好奇，捆绑作为一种长期制胜的战略，你怎么看？还有，你怎么跟比如微软这种有一天可能把你产品免费捆绑进去、而你可能大难临头的公司竞争？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I think it's two separate questions, so let me take them separately. The first is, what do I think about bundling? So small and medium-sized companies will go from being a single product company to a multi-product company in order to progress. Because you need a diversified financial model, because you need to be able to sell new products into your customer base who should already be friendly to you if they like your products. And because you need to really expand your total addressable market to get to be $1 billion or $2 billion company. But I believe in bundling is a growth strategy. (00:53:57): Specifically for product led growth companies, bundling is not a great land strategy. So at Atlassian, we had a number of products and experimented with different bundled lands. And it really slowed down the product led growth motion. So we ended up going back to land with a single product, high velocity, single person uses it quickly starts to get value, and then come in with other things. (00:54:22): So from that perspective, product led growth bundling is not very effective. Bundling for a sales led motion is pretty effective when you're at the right stage of growth. (00:54:33): And then as far as the question of competing against Microsoft, there's these two parts of the philosophies. A best of breed and an all in one. An Oracle was an all in one, and Microsoft is an all in one. You can buy all the things and your CFO can get a discount by spending a whole bunch of money on a bunch of things. But in the all-in one, some of the pieces aren't as good as the best of breed. (00:54:57): And so Slack for a long time was the best of breed. People were willing to pay more because they thought it was markedly better than the other instant messaging options. (00:55:07): But there's shifts between best of breed and all in one in economic wins. So right now, CFOs are putting the squeeze. Is Slack really that much better than Microsoft if the Microsoft one is free with all of our other purchases? It's tough. It's tough to go head-to-head with a powerful, big investing, all-in-one competitor. The only way to win is to be the best and have a product that's so much better, that it's worth the extra money.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是两个独立的问题，所以我分开说。第一，我怎么看捆绑？中小公司为了往前走，会从单一产品公司变成多产品公司。因为你需要多元化的财务模型，因为你需要能把新产品卖进你的客户群——如果他们喜欢你的产品，本该对你友好；还因为你需要真的扩大你的总可寻址市场（TAM），才能成为 10 亿、20 亿美元的公司。所以我相信捆绑是个增长战略。（00:53:57）具体对产品驱动增长公司来说，捆绑不是个好的"切入"（land）战略。在 Atlassian，我们有好几款产品，也试过不同的捆绑切入。它真的拖慢了产品驱动增长。所以我们最后回到：用单一产品切入，高速度，让单个人快速用上、快速获得价值，然后再带进别的东西。（00:54:22）所以从那个角度看，产品驱动增长的捆绑不太有效。在正确的增长阶段，销售驱动的捆绑相当有效。（00:54:33）然后关于跟微软竞争的问题，这里有两种哲学：best of breed（同类最佳）和 all-in-one（全家桶）。Oracle 是全家桶，微软也是全家桶。你可以买所有东西，你的 CFO 因为花了一大笔钱买一堆东西而拿到折扣。但在全家桶里，有些部件不如同类最佳。（00:54:57）所以 Slack 长期是同类最佳。人们愿意付更多，因为他们觉得它明显比别的即时通讯选项好。（00:55:07）但同类最佳和全家桶之间，会随着经济胜负而切换。所以现在，CFO 们在施压。如果微软那个是跟我们其他采购一起免费送的，Slack 真的有那么好过微软吗？很难。正面硬刚一个强大的、大把砸钱的全家桶对手，很难。唯一的赢法，就是做到最好、有个好到值得多花钱的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So essentially in a tough environment, bundling is most effective almost. And then this other interesting point about [inaudible 00:55:47], you want to stay focused on one specific pain point. What is it that Atlassian tried to do that they tried to pitch all your planning products in one suite? Is that kind of what we-
turns.zh: 有意思。所以本质上在艰难环境里，捆绑几乎是最有效的。然后另一个关于[听不清 00:55:47]的有趣点，你要聚焦在一个具体的痛点上。Atlassian 当时试着做的，是不是想把你们所有规划产品打包在一个套件里推？就是我们——

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Well, Jira was the issue tracking. And then we also had Confluence, which was the Wiki page. So let's say there was a business bundle that could have been HipChat, Confluence and Jira. Or there were developer combinations that could have been Jira, Bitbucket, and maybe Confluence too for an engineering team. (00:56:19): Basically, if you have to evaluate multiple products to purchase something, it's not a fast and easy online self-service buy. Because you're like, "Do I need all three products? Can I break them apart? Do they all work? Are each of them best of breed?" Whereas if you're like, "I need issue tracking, I'm going to buy Jira, this looks good. I've tried it out, I'm ready to go." That can happen in seven days. Whereas if you add in multiple products, it takes more days and just leads to fewer conversions.
turns.zh: 嗯，Jira 是问题追踪。然后我们还有 Confluence，那个维基页面。所以假设有个商务套件可以是 HipChat、Confluence 和 Jira。或者给工程团队的开发者组合：Jira、Bitbucket，可能还有 Confluence。（00:56:19）基本上，如果你得评估多个产品才能买个东西，那它就不是个快速轻松的在线自助购买。因为你会想"我需要这三款全要吗？能拆开吗？它们都好用吗？每个都是同类最佳吗？"而如果你是"我需要问题追踪，我要买 Jira，看着不错。我试过了，准备上手。"那七天就能成。而如果你加进多款产品，要多花好几天，只会带来更低的转化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes absolute sense. I can see someone thinking the complete opposite and then now realizing how we see. I see why this isn't working.
turns.zh: 这完全说得通。我能想象有人想的正相反，然后现在意识到我们怎么看。我懂为什么这不灵了。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: You should always test it. Right? I mean, the secret to product led growth is can you test it? And so we tested everything. We tried bundles. We didn't try bundles. We tried different things in the bundles. We tried different days. Data led insights are better than anything any pundits would say on a podcast.
turns.zh: 你永远该去测试。对吧？我的意思是，产品驱动增长的秘密是：你能测试吗？所以我们什么都测。我们试过捆绑。我们也没试捆绑。我们在捆绑里试过不同的东西。我们试过不同的日子。数据带来的洞察，比任何专家在播客上说的都强。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Well with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那说到这，我们到了超刺激的闪电回合。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What are two or three books that you recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好。你最经常推荐给别人的是哪两三本书？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: The number one book is a life book called Tao Te Ching, the Stephen Mitchell translation. And the Tao Te Ching is a philosophy about the flow of life. And I love it. I've carried the Pocket Guide with me for 25 years. (00:57:40): The second one is business focused. Never Split the Difference, which is a great book about negotiating written by a former CIA hostage negotiator, which also helps me with negotiations at work and with my children. So that's a great book.
turns.zh: 第一本是本人生书，叫《道德经》（Tao Te Ching），Stephen Mitchell 的译本。道德经是关于生命之流的哲学。我超爱。这本口袋本我带了 25 年。（00:57:40）第二本是偏商业的。《永远别把差价平分》（Never Split the Difference），是位前 CIA 人质谈判专家写的关于谈判的好书，也帮我处理工作里、跟孩子们的谈判。所以那是本好书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually, I've been trying to read that book on audio. What's something you've taken away from me? Because the stories are so interesting and I'm always like, "What should I actually do in my day-to-day life?" What stuck with you?
turns.zh: 其实我一直在听那本书的有声版。你从里面带走的是什么？因为那些故事太有趣了，我总在想"我在日常生活里到底该怎么做？"什么印在你脑子里了？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: It's kind of the obvious thing that I wasn't good at. It's that you just really want to put yourself so deeply in the shoes of the other person, that you can figure out what make the win for both of you, right? Basically he says, "You can't win the negotiation by strong arming what you want. You really get to get to a win-win," which is probably every negotiation book ever. But he texturizes it so much. So I just felt like I was really able to... In my last office, we moved last year. I actually had the CliffNotes of his book printed out and posted on my wall because he had a series of questions to help you get deeper and deeper into the mindset behind people. (00:58:49): And connected, but not connected the book How To Win Friends and Influence People, that's the 1932 bestseller, is basically that. People don't want to hear about you. They want you to be thinking about them. And then you can make friends with them, or you can negotiate with them, or you can get your hostage back.
turns.zh: 是那种我本来不擅长的显而易见的东西。就是你要真的把自己深深放进对方的鞋里，才能想出对你们双方都赢的办法，对吧？基本上他说："你不能靠强压你想要的东西来赢谈判。你真的要达成双赢。"这可能每本谈判书都讲。但他把它讲得太有层次了。所以我真的觉得自己能……我上个办公室，我们去年搬的。我其实把他那本书的精华打印出来贴墙上了，因为他有一系列问题帮你在人们心态背后越钻越深。（00:58:49）连起来——但没连上的书是《如何赢得朋友并影响他人》（How To Win Friends and Influence People），那是 1932 年的畅销书，本质就是这个。人们不想听你讲自己。他们想让你想着他们。然后你能跟他们做朋友、能跟他们谈判、能把你的人质带回来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I read How to Win Friends and Influence People when I was very young. And specifically, the chapters about there's no better sound in the world to someone than their name. Carilu.
turns.zh: 我很小的时候读过《如何赢得朋友并影响他人》。特别是那些章节，说对一个人来说，世上最好听的声音没有比他自己的名字更好的了。Carilu。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: It's true. Thank you. You said it correctly.
turns.zh: 真的。谢谢。你发音对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, moving on. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 好，继续。最近最爱的电影或剧？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: My favorite movie is Everything Everywhere All at Once. It's basically a sci-fi about all the different ways your life could turn out if you made different choices. And it was really a mind bender that made me think about all the different ways tiny decisions have changed my life, but then also an appreciation for the life that you have. At the end, it doesn't ruin the story, but she has this love of what she has, even though it's not as good or as different as some of the other options.
turns.zh: 我最爱的电影是《瞬息全宇宙》（Everything Everywhere All at Once）。基本是个科幻，讲如果你做了不同选择，你人生所有可能走向。它真的让我脑筋急转弯，想到那些微小的决定怎么改变了我的人生，但也让我对现在拥有的这个人生生出感恩。结尾不剧透，但她爱她所拥有的，即使它不如某些别的选项好、或不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我超爱。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: So I bought this poster. I don't think you can see it on the bath, but it says, "Gratitude turns what we have into enough."
turns.zh: 所以我买了这张海报。我觉得你在澡盆上可能看不到，上面写："感恩把我们拥有的变成足够。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very Buddhist.
turns.zh: 很佛教。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I like it. Read the Tao Te Ching.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。去读道德经。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not a Post-it, but art. Another teaching from Carilu. I think this needs to be a second newsletter of yours. Life advice.
turns.zh: 不是便利贴，是艺术品。又一个 Carilu 的教导。我觉得这得成为你的第二份 newsletter。人生建议。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Which is funny. I've been thinking about that one. It would be called The Tao of Hypergrowth.
turns.zh: 有意思。我一直在想那个。它会叫《超增长的道》（The Tao of Hypergrowth）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. I love that.
turns.zh: 天哪。我太爱了。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: And actually, I was thinking about doing it and taking actual clips from the Tao Te Ching, and doing textural analysis about how it applies to our. I've been thinking about this actual podcast for a while because I used to want to do the... I mean blog, the Tao of Parenthood. Because basically parenting, you try to control and fix all the things you didn't do right in your life. But actually, it's the act of providing freedom that lets them go out and explore and then come back to your way of being. So, I don't know. The Tao Te Ching, I love it.
turns.zh: 其实我一直在想做它，从道德经里取真实片段，做文本分析讲它怎么应用到我们的……我想这期播客想了一阵了，因为我以前想做……我是说博客，《为人父母的道》（The Tao of Parenthood）。因为基本上，育儿，是你试图控制和修好你人生里没做对的那些事。但其实，正是给予自由这件事，让他们出去探索、再回到你的生活方式。所以，我不知道。道德经，我超爱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see so many opportunities. You got to stop what you're doing. Just write all these things.
turns.zh: 我看到太多机会了。你得停下手头事。把这些全写出来。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: I know. But I love the hypergrowth customers, clients.
turns.zh: 我知道。但我爱超增长的客户、顾问们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Next question. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask?
turns.zh: 好。下一个问题。你最喜欢问的一个面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: So this is a little heavy, but it actually is my favorite. It's, "How many people have you fired? And tell me about each of the experiences." So the reason I ask this question is because generally, I'm managing teams of managers. And generally, I need people who have managed many people for a longer period of time. Or even if they're junior managers, how long and how many people they've managed is indicated by how many people they've fired. Because if you've never fired anyone, then you haven't managed very many people for very long, unfortunately. (01:01:39): And firing people is the hardest part of a leader's career. So how they talk about it, their compassion, and their need to drive the business, and the circumstances, "Was it layoffs? How did that work? Did you have to performance manage someone out? How did it work? Did you just have to restructure the team because of business goals? How did it work?" Gives you a lot of insight into their experience and their humanity in a way that they're not prepared for. So you really get the real story, and get a sense for what they would be like as a leader under a lot of pressure and difficult situations.
turns.zh: 这个有点重，但它真的是我的最爱。就是："你炒过多少人？跟我讲讲每一次的经历。"我问这个问题的原因是：一般来说，我管的是经理们的团队。一般来说，我需要那些管了很多人、管了挺长时间的人。或者即使是初级经理，他们管了多久、管了多少人，从他们炒过多少人就能看出来。因为如果你从没炒过人，那不幸的是，你没管过很多人、也没管很久。（01:01:39）而炒人，是领导者职业生涯里最难的部分。所以他们怎么讲、他们的同理心、他们推动业务的必要性，以及当时的情形——"是裁员吗？怎么操作的？你得把某人绩效管走吗？怎么操作的？你只是因为业务目标要重组团队吗？怎么操作的？"——这能给你很多洞察，进到他们的经验、他们的人性里，而且他们没准备。所以你真能拿到真实故事，感觉到他们在高压和困难情境下会是个什么样的领导。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've never heard that one before and I love it. Reminds me of a episode with Matt Mochary where we talk about how to lay people off really successfully and elegantly.
turns.zh: 我从没听过这个，我超爱。让我想起跟 Matt Mochary 那期，我们聊怎么把裁员做得真的成功、优雅。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: It's a hard.
turns.zh: 那是很难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Next question. What's a favorite product that you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 对。下一个问题。你最近发现、并且超爱的一个产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: So I follow my favorite products to the companies that I advise. I love 1Password. I've got my 85-year-old grandfather and all of my family and friends set up on it. I love the cross-platform nature. (01:02:45): I love Miro and whiteboards. I joined Productboard because of this cross-company alignment and views into what's coming up on the roadmap, which is really the most important thing for the company. Momentum, as we talked about, having a great product and a great product strategy. (01:03:02): And then I'm dabbling in all the AI things. I want to be excellent in AI visualization and art. I'm experimenting with Midjourney, but still kind of flailing. I've hired my 13-year old as my strategic advisor. And yeah, I'd love to work for OpenAI and ChatGPT. It's really interesting.
turns.zh: 我跟着我爱的产品走到我顾问的公司。我爱 1Password。我把我 85 岁的爷爷、还有我所有家人朋友都设上了。我爱它的跨平台特性。（01:02:45）我爱 Miro 和白板。我加入 Productboard 是因为这种跨公司对齐、以及能看到路线图要出什么——那对公司真的才是最重要的事。我们聊过的势头，有个好产品和好产品战略。（01:03:02）然后我在捣鼓所有 AI 的东西。我想在 AI 可视化和艺术上做到出色。我在试 Midjourney，但还有点瞎扑腾。我雇了我 13 岁的娃当我的战略顾问。对，我超想去 OpenAI 和 ChatGPT 工作。真的有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something relatively minor that you've changed in the way a product is built or just the company operates, that has led to tremendous impact on their ability to execute?
turns.zh: 有什么相对小的改变，你在一个产品的构建方式、或者公司运作方式上做的，却对他们执行能力造成了巨大影响？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: On the product side, one of the concepts that I really like is the Amazon concept around writing the press release at the beginning of a product ideation. So one of the issues between marketing and product is the product will work so hard on something, and there'll be lots of different features, that it won't really be a theme that the marketing team can talk about. And then someone hands it to marketing and says, "Make this marketable." One of my mentors had this comment, "It's a bag of doorknobs." What do I do with this bag of doorknobs? Who wants to buy a bag of doorknobs? They want to buy the door and the concept. (01:04:13): So I like this idea of writing a press release. Start with the end in mind, and then negotiate. Is this good enough? Will this really resonate? Or is this really what we're trying to build? Or is this really the outcome we're trying to get with the product? So I've heard about Amazon do it. We experimented with it at Classy. I haven't done it at mass scale, but I love the concept.
turns.zh: 产品侧，我超爱的一个概念，是亚马逊那个在产品构思之初就写新闻稿的概念。所以营销和产品之间的一个问题就是：产品会在一个东西上死磕，会有很多不同的功能，以至于它其实没有一个营销团队能讲的主题。然后有人把它交给营销说"把这个变得能卖。"我的一个导师有句评论："这是一袋门把手。"我拿这袋门把手干嘛？谁想买一袋门把手？人们想买的是那扇门、那个概念。（01:04:13）所以我喜欢写新闻稿这个点子。以终为始，然后去协商。这够好吗？真能打动人吗？还是我们真想建的？还是我们真想用这产品拿到的成果？所以我听过亚马逊这么做。我们在 Classy 试过。我还没大规模做过，但我爱这个概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. I know you're a meditator. We've talked a little bit about your Buddhist nature. What's one tip for people that have been trying to meditate and just can't make it happen? What's your one tip for helping people meditate more often?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。我知道你是冥想者。我们聊过一点你佛教的气质。对那些一直想冥想、就是做不到的人，你的一条建议是什么？你帮人们更常冥想的一条建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: So I'm a cheater because I was groomed to meditate. I don't remember how early, but I remember that the first meditations my mom had me listen to was a rainbow butterfly as I fell asleep when I was in kindergarten. (01:04:55): So I've been meditating my whole life, with mixed success. And the real secret is just that there's no right way, that there's no wrong way. That it's just making the time to be present, and breathe, and sense, and be here now. (01:05:13): And so I use guided meditations mostly, because I'm not the best at quieting my own mind. I'm thrifty. So I use some free meditations. I use Tara Brach, who's a great meditator, who has short and long concept meditations. (01:05:30): And I like this old one called Meditation Oasis, which actually isn't in publishing anymore, but it's still a podcast. And I re-listen to all theirs over and over. So stick with it is the secret to meditation, and any benefits you get from being present in meditation, hopefully carry over to be being present in life.
turns.zh: 我算是个作弊的人，因为我是被"培养"出来冥想的。我不记得多早了，但我记得我妈让我听的第一批冥想，是我幼儿园快睡着时听的彩虹蝴蝶。（01:04:55）所以我这辈子都在冥想，成效时好时坏。真正的秘密就是：没有正确的方式，也没有错误的方式。就是腾出时间，去临在、去呼吸、去感知、去"此时此地"。（01:05:13）所以我大多用引导冥想，因为我不擅长让自己的心静下来。我挺省钱的。所以我用一些免费的冥想。我用 Tara Brach，她是个很棒的冥想者，有短有长的概念冥想。（01:05:30）我还喜欢一个老的叫 Meditation Oasis 的，其实它已经不出版了，但还是有播客。我把他们所有的都反复听。所以坚持，就是冥想的秘密；而你在冥想临在中得到的任何好处，希望都能延续到生活中的临在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My whole body just relaxed as you were talking through all that. So you have a skill. Carilu, this was amazing. We learned how to grow products, how to live better lives, how to become more mindful. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to learn more, reach out? And/or how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 你讲这些的时候，我整个身体都放松了。所以你是有本事的。Carilu，这期太棒了。我们学会了怎么增长产品、怎么活更好、怎么更觉知。最后两个问题。如果大家想多了解、想联系，网上哪里能找到你？以及/或者，听众怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Follow me on LinkedIn, or I have a new blog carilu.com on Substack. Thanks to Lenny for the inspiration. And I still have one more advisory slot open, and I'd love to work with more AI companies. I just joined Weights & Biases in the ML op space. But if you know of other great scale up AI companies, I'd love to help junior marketing executives or first time founders see what the next stage of growth looks like and get there.
turns.zh: 在 LinkedIn 上关注我，或者我有在 Substack 上的新博客 carilu.com。谢谢 Lenny 的启发。我还剩一个顾问名额空着，我很想跟更多 AI 公司合作。我刚加入了 ML ops 领域的 Weights & Biases。但如果你知道其他很棒的规模化 AI 公司，我很乐意帮初级营销高管、或者第一次当创始人的人，看清下一个增长阶段长什么样、并到达那里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And again, if they are interested in that, how do they reach out to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。再说一次，如果他们感兴趣，怎么联系你？

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: On LinkedIn or through carilu.com.
turns.zh: 通过 LinkedIn 或者 carilu.com。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Carilu, thank you again so much for making time and for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Carilu，再次非常感谢你抽时间、来到这里。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请我，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bye everyone.
turns.zh: 大家再见。

turns.speaker: Carilu Dietrich
turns.en: Bye.
turns.zh: 再见。

turns.zh: 非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这期有价值，可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅本节目。也请考虑给我们评分或留个评论，因为这真的能帮其他听众找到这档播客。你可以在 lennyspodcast.com 找到所有往期节目或了解更多关于本节目。下期见。
